summary: An IPng white paper analyzing BSD host implementation, written to give engineers a BSD reference point while choosing an IPng proposal. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A paper checking how hard it would be to add a new Internet design to one popular operating system.

subtitle: Engineering analysis of how to add a new Internet protocol to BSD operating systems.

tldr.problem: Deploying IPng on existing BSD operating systems would require substantial changes to network software architecture, APIs, socket structures, and protocol implementations while maintaining compatibility with IPv4 applications.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes the BSD network software architecture—including interprocess communications, the network subsystem, protocol layers, and data link layer—then identifies specific alterations needed at each layer and new capabilities required for IPng support.
tldr.outcome: The analysis provided implementers a reference point for understanding the scope of work needed to support IPv6 on BSD systems and highlighted the importance of maintaining application compatibility during the transition.

facts.label: Network software component layers
facts.value: 6 (application, IPC, transport, network, link, data link)

today: RFC 1682 is an informational document reflecting 1994 implementation perspectives. The BSD community's actual implementation of IPv6 support followed many of these principles, and the dual-stack transition model described became standard practice across operating systems. The RFC's emphasis on maintaining application compatibility proved prescient, as backwards compatibility was crucial to successful IPv6 deployment.

sections.title: Introduction and BSD Architecture Overview
sections.content:
This white paper provides engineering analysis of IPng implementation on BSD hosts. The author examines the BSD network software architecture as a reference point for understanding implementation considerations when deploying IPng.

The BSD network software architecture consists of three tightly coupled components: the interprocess communications (IPC) facility, the network communications subsystem, and the network protocols. The IPC facility includes both user-space APIs (sockets interface) and kernel-space components that applications use to access network features.

The network subsystem comprises four logical layers: transport layer (TCP and UDP), network layer (IPv4 modules, routing protocols), link-dependent layer (ARP, address resolution), and data link layer (Ethernet, FDDI, ATM, HIPPI, PPP). Applications use socket APIs, DNS (BIND), and SNMP management to interact with the network stack.
sections.eli5: BSD operating systems have a standard way to organize network code in layers, from applications at the top down to hardware at the bottom. The paper explains how each layer would need to change for a new Internet protocol.

sections.title: Network Software Alterations Required
sections.content:
Applications embedding IPv4 addresses: Applications that hardcode IPv4 addresses in datagram payloads assume address format stability. FTP is identified as a major protocol with this problem, requiring special handling when addresses change.

Transport interfaces and APIs: Network APIs must be enhanced to support larger IPng addresses and to differentiate between IPv4 and IPv6 address requests to BIND DNS. The way socket address structures are implemented affects whether existing IPv4 applications must be recompiled.

Socket layer and structures: The socket layer must be modified to support IPng network addresses and incorporate new or removed options and services into the socket abstraction.

Transport layer: TCP and UDP implementations must be modified to support new services proposed by IPng. The transport layer becomes more complex, selecting between IPv4 or IPng network layer components. Maintaining the performance improvements from hundreds of man-years of TCP/UDP optimization is critical.

Network layer components: The greatest alterations occur here. A host must maintain an integrated network layer supporting either IPv4 or IPng below the transport layer. Depending on the IPng proposal, changes range from complete protocol replacement to extensions of existing IPv4 protocols.

Link-dependent layer: Must accommodate new IPng addresses and support system discovery models defined by IPng proposals. Connection discovery, address resolution, and interface management all require modifications.
sections.eli5: Every part of the network stack—from applications down to hardware drivers—would need changes: APIs for address sizes, new data structures, modified protocols, and discovery mechanisms.

sections.title: Extended Capabilities and Features
sections.content:
Beyond basic alterations, BSD hosts would gain extended capabilities with IPng:

Autoconfiguration and autoregistration: Hosts must support configuration for both IPv4 and new IPng addresses, plus the BOOTP protocol used for diskless systems.

Path MTU discovery: Mechanisms for discovering the maximum transmission unit along a path require alterations from IPv4 implementations due to system discovery changes.

Multicast: Each IPng proposal includes alterations to multicast functionality, with IPv4 unicast broadcast potentially replaced by multicast broadcast.

Flow specification and handling: All IPng proposals include mechanisms for applications to specify traffic characteristics and requirements.

System discovery: Each proposal defines a new model for discovering hosts on networks and across internetworks, replacing ARP mechanisms.

Translation and encapsulation: Routing abstractions must handle potential translation or encapsulation of network layer datagrams required by IPng proposals.

Network layer security: Security mechanisms required at the network layer must be implemented by BSD hosts.

Network APIs and management: APIs must be enhanced to support new options and services. Network management must support new objects defined by IPng and handle altered network kernel data structures from new protocol datagrams.
sections.eli5: BSD would get new features like automatic address setup, multicast support, security in the network layer, and tools to monitor and manage the new protocol.

sections.title: Transition Software and Coexistence
sections.content:
Transition software enables BSD hosts to run both IPv4 and IPng simultaneously during migration. The RFC identifies twelve key areas requiring transition support:

DNS record handling must differentiate between IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. SNMP monitoring must manage both IPv4 and IPv6 network structures. APIs must support application-level IPv4/IPv6 selection. Standard networking tools (tcpdump, traceroute, netstat, ifconfig) must be adapted. Address resolution transitions from ARP to new system discovery mechanisms.

Configuration management, routing protocols, system discovery mechanisms, and socket address structures must all support dual-stack operation. The RFC emphasizes that existing IPv4 applications should not require recompilation when a host implements both network layers.

The RFC states that complete technical specifications must be available for any IPng proposal, with multiple implementations possible. It argues that existing IPv4 infrastructure is large and migration funding is limited, necessitating coexistence planning.
sections.eli5: During the switch from IPv4 to IPv6, old and new systems need to work together. This means old applications shouldn't break, routing works for both, and management tools understand both protocols.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that IPng proposals must include complete technical specifications and deployment plans. The IPng Directorate should review proposed specifications for completeness and detail.

A critical deployment variable is how long CIDR IPv4 address extension can maintain the viability of IPv4. This affects the time available for IPng development and deployment, and shapes transition planning requirements.

The RFC states clear requirements: IPng proposals should accommodate multiple implementations, there should be no requirement for hosts to support both IPv4 and IPng simultaneously, but deployment must be feasible given the existing large IPv4 infrastructure.
sections.eli5: Before picking a new Internet protocol, planners need to know exactly how to deploy it, how long IPv4 can stretch, and what multiple vendors will commit to building.
